summary: Defines how SNMP messages are carried over various underlying protocols. It separates the SNMP message format from the transport used to deliver it, so the same messages can travel over different networks. It replaces RFC 1906.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3417 explains how SNMP management messages travel over different network transports. It specifies address formats, well-known ports or sockets, message-size requirements and a shared encoding method. UDP over IPv4 is the preferred mapping for systems that support IPv4.

questions: what is the minimum snmp message size
subtitle: How SNMP messages are encoded and carried over several network transport protocols.

tldr.problem: SNMP management messages need to travel over network protocols without making their content depend on a particular transport. Implementations also need agreed address formats, endpoints and minimum message sizes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3417 defines how to encode an SNMP message into a single datagram or transport data unit for UDP over IPv4, OSI, AppleTalk DDP and IPX. The mappings use the same Basic Encoding Rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3417 is Internet Standard STD 62 and replaces RFC 1906; the protocol is unchanged from that RFC. UDP over IPv4 is the preferred mapping, and RFC 3417 has been updated by RFC 4789 and RFC 5590.

today: RFC 3417 is Internet Standard STD 62 and obsoletes RFC 1906. It has been updated by RFC 4789 and RFC 5590.

sections.title: Separating SNMP Messages from Transport
sections.content:
The Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) accesses managed objects stored in a Management Information Base (MIB). RFC 3417 defines how SNMP messages can be carried over several protocol suites, while the message operations themselves are specified separately in RFC 3416.

UDP over IPv4 is the preferred mapping. A system that implements IPv4 MUST implement it, and a system supporting another mapping SHOULD also provide it to improve interoperability. The RFC defines mappings for OSI, AppleTalk DDP and IPX as well.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP uses messages to read and manage network objects, and those messages can travel over different network protocols. Systems that support IPv4 must provide the UDP-over-IPv4 mapping.

sections.title: Transport Domains and Address Formats
sections.content:
The SNMPv2-TM module assigns a transport-domain identifier to each mapping and defines how transport addresses are written as octet strings. A UDP-over-IPv4 address is six octets: four for the IP address and two for the UDP port, in network byte order.

An OSI address contains a length, an NSAP address and a transport selector. An AppleTalk address contains a name with object, type and zone strings. An IPX address contains a network number, physical address and socket number in a 12-octet value. The module also retains a deprecated domain for proxying to SNMPv1 over UDP over IPv4.
sections.plainLanguage: Each transport has its own address format, so the SNMP module defines how to store each one. For example, an IPv4 transport address combines the network address and UDP port in six octets.

sections.title: SNMP over UDP over IPv4
sections.content:
For this mapping, each SNMP message is encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and sent in one UDP datagram over IPv4. An administrator is advised to configure command responders to listen on UDP port 161 and notification receivers on UDP port 162.

An entity using this mapping must accept messages up to and including 484 octets. Accepting messages up to 1472 octets is recommended, and support for larger messages is encouraged when possible.
sections.plainLanguage: Each SNMP message goes in one UDP datagram, with the same encoding rules used by the other mappings. Command responders use port 161, notification receivers use port 162, and devices must accept messages of at least 484 octets.

sections.title: OSI, AppleTalk and IPX Mappings
sections.content:
The OSI mapping places one SNMP message in one connectionless transport service data unit. It uses suggested transport selectors for command responders and notification receivers, and entities must accept at least 484 octets. The AppleTalk DDP mapping sends one message in a DDP datagram using protocol type 8; responders use socket 8 and notification receivers use socket 9.

AppleTalk nodes are identified by stable NBP names because their network addresses can change. Implementations use NBP lookups to resolve names, and the RFC recommends caching results and using lookups sparingly. The IPX mapping sends one message in a single IPX datagram with packet type 4. Its suggested sockets are 36879 and 36880, and the minimum accepted message is 546 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP can also use OSI, AppleTalk DDP and IPX, with one message in each transport unit. AppleTalk uses stable names that are looked up and cached, while the other mappings use their own transport addresses and endpoints.

sections.title: Encoding Messages with BER
sections.content:
All the mappings serialize messages using the Basic Encoding Rules for ASN.1. RFC 3417 restricts BER so that encoded data is interpreted consistently: lengths use the definite form, simple types use primitive encoding, and structured types use constructed encoding.

Values described with the ASN.1 BITS construct are encoded as an OCTET STRING. Named bits are placed from the high-order bit downward, and unused bits at the end are zero when sent and ignored when received. These rules apply to message wrappers, protocol data units and the objects they contain.
sections.plainLanguage: Every transport mapping uses the same strict rules to encode an SNMP message. These rules specify how lengths, simple values, structures and bit fields are represented so different systems can read them consistently.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that SNMPv1 alone is not a secure environment. Even if a network uses a protection mechanism such as IPsec, that does not determine which users may read or change objects through an SNMP command responder.

Implementers are advised to consider the SNMPv3 User-based Security Model in RFC 3414 and View-based Access Control Model in RFC 3415. The customer or user is responsible for configuring access so only authorized principals can read or change managed objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Protecting the network connection alone does not decide who may read or change managed objects. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 security features and careful access configuration.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1906
sections.content: RFC 3417 obsoletes RFC 1906. It says the changes are editorial improvements only and that the protocol is unchanged. The transport mappings and their operation remain the same.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC replaces RFC 1906 with editorial improvements. The protocol itself did not change.
